relationship: Shelter from hostile human speech and plotting
rationale: Both describe God sheltering people from hostile human activity. Psalm 30 joins concealment in God's presence with shelter from contradicting tongues; Psalm 63 follows its conspiracy with tongue-as-weapon imagery.

relationship: The tongue pictured as a sharp sword
rationale: Both turn the enemy's tongue into a sharp sword and place it alongside weapon imagery. Psalm 63 describes sharpening tongues; Psalm 56 identifies the tongue itself as the sword.

relationship: Concealed archery against the upright
rationale: Both describe enemies shooting an upright person from concealment: hidden places here and moonless darkness in Psalm 10. The bow, hidden attack and morally described victim form the particular parallel.

relationship: Wrongdoers suppose their actions are unseen
rationale: The plotters conceal traps and ask who will see them. Psalm 93 records evildoers denying that the Lord sees, then answers by appealing to the Maker of the eye. The texts compare presumed invisibility without identifying their offenders.

relationship: The deep human heart and divine examination
rationale: Psalm 63 places a human being and a deep heart after the failed search for lawless deeds. Jeremiah likewise calls the heart deep and a human hard to know, then declares the Lord's examination. The comparison preserves Psalm 63's unusual sequence without replacing it with another edition's wording.

relationship: The defeat of a tongue that claimed power
rationale: Psalm 63 says the adversaries' tongues grew powerless. Psalm 11 prays for the destruction of deceitful lips and the boasting tongue that claimed mastery. The correspondence is the reversal of hostile verbal power.

relationship: Witnessed divine deliverance produces fear
rationale: After the enemies' defeat, observers fear and announce God's acts. Exodus describes Israel seeing the Lord's defeat of Egypt and consequently fearing and trusting Him. This is a narrative illustration of that response, without identifying the psalm's unnamed conflict as the sea crossing.

relationship: The righteous and upright rejoice in the Lord
rationale: Both join rejoicing in the Lord with the righteous and those upright in heart. Psalm 63 adds hope and being praised; Psalm 31 commands exultation and boasting.

relationship: Vows repaid at the Lord's house in Jerusalem
rationale: Both locate repayment of a vow in Jerusalem and the Lord's worship. Psalm 115 explicitly places the vow before the people in the house's courts, corresponding to Psalm 64's hymn and vow in Zion and Jerusalem.

relationship: All flesh coming before God
rationale: The psalm joins its prayer with all flesh coming to God. Isaiah likewise speaks of all flesh coming before Him to bow in Jerusalem, with monthly and Sabbath observance specified there.

relationship: God asked to deal mercifully with communal sins
rationale: Psalm 64 acknowledges overpowering lawless deeds and says God will make atonement for impieties. Psalm 78 asks the saving God to be propitious toward the community's sins. The comparison concerns divine action toward confessed communal wrongdoing.

relationship: Blessedness of dwelling in God's house
rationale: Both pronounce blessed the person or people dwelling in God's courts or house. Psalm 64 stresses divine choice and being filled with the house's good things; Psalm 83 describes the inhabitants' continuing praise.

relationship: Hope in God's salvation reaches distant nations and islands
rationale: The psalm calls God the hope of earth's ends and those far away at sea. Isaiah connects outgoing salvation with nations and islands waiting and hoping in God's arm. Both extend hope beyond the immediate land community.

relationship: Mountains assigned their place by God
rationale: Psalm 64 describes God preparing mountains in His strength. Psalm 103 describes mountains rising to the place He founded for them. Both place the mountains' establishment under God's ordering of the earth.

relationship: God stirs the sea and its sounding waves
rationale: The psalm says God troubles the sea's hollow and its waves' sounds. Isaiah identifies Him as the God who stirs the sea and makes its waves resound. Neither text is rewritten as a statement that He calms the water.

relationship: Watering the earth produces food
rationale: God's water enriches the earth and prepares food in Psalm 64. Psalm 103 joins watering the mountains and filling the earth with the production of plants and bread. The connection is the stated water-to-food provision.

relationship: Heavenly water makes the soil sprout
rationale: The psalm asks for drenched furrows and rejoicing growth in drops of water. Isaiah describes rain and snow drenching the earth, making it sprout and yield seed and food. The literal agricultural process supplies Isaiah's following analogy for God's word.

relationship: Divine care for rain-fed land throughout the year
rationale: The psalm blesses the year's crown of divine kindness and rich plains. Deuteronomy describes hills and plains drinking heaven's rain under God's care from the year's beginning to its end. Both connect annual divine care with the land's fertility.

relationship: The wilderness becomes fruitful and rejoices
rationale: Both picture wilderness places transformed into fruitful abundance and exultation. The psalm gives rich wilderness places and rejoicing hills; Isaiah commands the thirsty wilderness and desert places to flower and exult.

relationship: All the earth summoned to shout to God
rationale: The running text after Psalm 65's heading summons all the earth to shout to God, matching Psalm 99's summons to shout to the Lord. The heading Of resurrection is preserved without identifying a particular resurrection event.

relationship: Glory given in praise of God's name
rationale: Psalm 65 commands music to God's name and glory to His praise. Psalm 95 addresses the nations' families and commands glory for the Lord's name. The comparison joins the name and the commanded gift of glory.

relationship: Power is accompanied by the adversaries' lying
rationale: Psalm 65 says enemies will lie to God through His abundant power. Psalm 17 places foreigners' lying alongside the speaker's appointment over nations and their obedience. The actual language of lying is retained rather than converted into sincere submission.

relationship: Worldwide worship and glorification of God's name
rationale: Psalm 65 calls all the earth to bow and make music to God's name. Psalm 85 expects all the nations He made to come, bow before Him and glorify His name. The paired bowing and honoring the name form the correspondence.

relationship: The invitation to come and see God's works
rationale: Both explicitly invite listeners to come and see the Lord's works. Psalm 45 calls them wonders upon the earth, while Psalm 65 calls His counsels concerning humanity fearsome.

relationship: The sea made dry for Israel's passage
rationale: The psalm's sea turned into dry land corresponds to Exodus's account of the Lord making the sea dry and Israel entering on dry ground. This connection concerns the sea clause; the psalm's river clause is separately compared with Joshua.

relationship: Passage on foot through a river
rationale: The psalm speaks of passing through a river on foot. Joshua describes the priests and all Israel crossing the Jordan on dry ground. The river-crossing correspondence is kept distinct from the psalm's preceding sea image.

relationship: God observes peoples from His sovereign position
rationale: Psalm 65 joins God's rule with His eyes looking upon nations. Psalm 32 describes His heavenly observation of all humanity and understanding of their deeds. Both connect universal divine oversight with human conduct.

relationship: Nations and peoples called to praise
rationale: Psalm 65 addresses the nations and commands audible blessing of God. Psalm 116 likewise addresses all nations and peoples with a command to praise the Lord. Both broaden the worshipping audience beyond one people.

relationship: Life preserved and feet kept from slipping
rationale: Both join the preservation of the speaker's life with protection of the feet from slipping or shaking. Psalm 55 explicitly says rescue from death; Psalm 65 says God set the soul in life.

relationship: God tests His people as silver is refined
rationale: Both describe divine testing through fire by comparison with refining silver. Zechariah applies it to a remaining third and adds gold, while the psalm speaks of the praying community without that numerical identification.

relationship: Passing through both water and fire under God's care
rationale: The psalm recalls passing through fire and water and emerging into refreshment. Isaiah promises God's presence when crossing water and fire. The two hazards and divine preservation form the parallel without identifying a single historical passage.

relationship: Payment of vows within God's house
rationale: The speaker enters God's house and pays vows. Psalm 115 likewise locates paying vows to the Lord in the house's courts before the people. The vow and sanctuary setting are both explicit.

relationship: Distress, prayer and the repayment of vows
rationale: Psalm 65 identifies its vows as words spoken in affliction. Jonah's prayer begins with a cry from affliction and concludes with promised repayment of vows. The comparison follows the same distress-to-vow sequence without identifying the two speakers.

relationship: Livestock offered as whole burnt offerings
rationale: The psalm names oxen and other flock animals among its whole burnt offerings. Leviticus explicitly authorizes gifts from cattle and the flock and describes a cattle whole burnt offering. This supplies the ritual setting without claiming the law uses the psalm's marrow-rich description.

relationship: Same-chapter movement from seeing divine works to hearing personal testimony
rationale: Earlier in this same psalm the audience is invited to come and see God's works. Here those fearing God are invited to come and hear what He did for the speaker's soul. The changed sense and personal focus mark a distinct turn in the invitation.

relationship: Wrongdoing and the refusal of prayer
rationale: The psalm places regard for injustice in the heart under the condition that the Lord not hear. Isaiah refuses multiplied supplication from blood-filled hands and commands removal of evil and pursuit of justice. The parallel preserves the psalm's condition rather than declaring it a confession of actual injustice.

relationship: Blessing, mercy and the shining divine face
rationale: The psalm asks for divine compassion, blessing and a shining face, closely corresponding to the priestly blessing's mercy, blessing and shining face. Numbers also explicitly adds keeping and peace.

relationship: Salvation made known beyond Israel to the nations
rationale: The psalm seeks knowledge of God's way on earth and salvation among all nations. Isaiah appoints the servant as light for nations to bring salvation to the earth's extremity. The comparison concerns the stated international reach, without naming the psalm's speaker as that servant.

relationship: All peoples called into thanksgiving
rationale: The repeated invitation that all peoples thank God corresponds to Psalm 116's invitation that all peoples and nations praise Him. Both explicitly make every people the addressed worshipping body.

relationship: The nations rejoice before righteous judgment
rationale: Psalm 66 joins the nations' gladness with God's upright judgment. Psalm 95 similarly declares judgment of peoples with uprightness and surrounds the coming judgment with creation's rejoicing. Judgment and joy are linked in both passages.

relationship: Same-chapter refrain around the declaration of just rule
rationale: The line repeats verse 4's call for all peoples to thank God, enclosing verse 5's glad nations and upright judgment. This is an explicit structural refrain, not an additional historical event.

relationship: The land's produce as divine blessing
rationale: The psalm couples the earth giving fruit with a request for God's blessing. Leviticus promises rain, the land's produce and trees' fruit within its stated obedience condition. The agricultural blessing is compared without silently adding that condition to the psalm's line.

relationship: Fear of the Lord extended to the whole earth
rationale: Psalm 66 calls for all earth's ends to fear God; Psalm 32 commands all the earth and its inhabitants to fear Him. Both explicitly extend reverence to the entire inhabited world.

relationship: The ark-departure invocation echoed
rationale: The psalm's prayer for God to arise, scatter enemies and make His haters flee closely matches Moses' invocation when the ark sets out. The actual supplied Numbers reference is 10:34.

relationship: God's enemies vanish like smoke
rationale: Both use vanishing smoke to describe the end of God's enemies. Psalm 67 asks that they vanish; Psalm 36 describes the enemies and sinners vanishing after their exaltation.

relationship: Melting wax before the divine presence
rationale: Psalm 67 compares sinners perishing before God with wax melting before fire. Psalm 96 compares mountains melting before the Lord with wax. The shared melting image is retained while distinguishing the objects that melt.

relationship: Righteous people rejoice in the Lord's presence
rationale: Both specifically call the righteous to rejoice and exult in relation to God. Psalm 67 places their gladness before Him; Psalm 31 addresses the righteous and upright in heart.

relationship: Preparing a road for the Lord
rationale: Psalm 67 commands a road for the One whose name is Lord. Isaiah commands preparation of the Lord's way and straight paths for God. The road-making correspondence does not replace the psalm's rider upon the west with a different riding image.

relationship: God defends orphans and widows
rationale: The psalm names God Father of orphans and judge of widows. Deuteronomy explicitly describes His judgment for the orphan and widow. Both assign the protection of these vulnerable groups to God.

relationship: God releases people in fetters
rationale: Psalm 67 describes God leading the fettered out with courage, while Psalm 145 states that the Lord releases those in fetters. Other clauses about a house, one disposition and rebellious tomb-dwellers are not silently reinterpreted through this comparison.

relationship: God precedes His people in the wilderness
rationale: The psalm recalls God going before His people through the wilderness. Exodus narrates their wilderness encampment and God's cloud-and-fire guidance before them. The narrative supplies the concrete form of the guidance.

relationship: Shaking earth, dripping heavens and Sinai
rationale: Both poetic recollections join the earth shaking, heavenly water and Sinai before the God of Israel. Judges places the divine departure in Seir and Edom; the psalm preserves its own wilderness sequence.

relationship: Rain accompanies restoration after depletion
rationale: The psalm joins rain for the weakened inheritance with divine restoration. Joel joins renewed rainfall and full harvests with repayment of years consumed by locusts. The restoration-through-rain pattern is compared without identifying the psalm's weakness as that locust event.

relationship: Divine salvation announced as good news
rationale: Psalm 67 says the Lord will give an utterance to those announcing good news. Isaiah describes the good-news messenger and God's making salvation heard. The comparison is the divinely supplied proclamation, without importing a gender or number of messengers absent from the psalm's wording.

relationship: God chooses a dwelling and remains there
rationale: Psalm 67 speaks of the mountain in which God pleased to dwell and His continuing residence. Psalm 131 explicitly says God chose Zion for His dwelling and rest. The parallel is divine choice and enduring dwelling; it does not supply an unnamed mountain's identity merely from the shared theme.

relationship: Sinai and the Lord amid a vast heavenly company
rationale: Psalm 67 joins the Lord at Sinai with a ten-thousandfold chariot and thousands. Deuteronomy likewise places His coming from Sinai with myriads and angels at His right hand. The distinct descriptions of that company are preserved.

relationship: Ascension and captive-captivity wording with a changed gift action
rationale: Ephesians cites ascending on high and taking captivity captive, then interprets the ascent and descent in relation to Christ. The psalm says received gifts among humankind; Ephesians says gave gifts to human beings. That difference is retained rather than harmonized away.

relationship: The Lord and escape from death's boundary
rationale: Psalm 67 assigns the exits of death to the Lord. Psalm 9 addresses Him as the One raising the speaker from death's gates. The exit and gate images connect divine salvation with departure from death.

relationship: Divine judgment described as crushing heads
rationale: Psalm 67 says God will crush His enemies' heads. Psalm 109 describes the Lord crushing kings and heads in judgment among nations. The shared concrete judgment image is retained without identifying their enemies as one historical group.

relationship: Blood imagery following the enemies' defeat
rationale: Psalm 67 pictures a foot dipped in blood and dogs' tongues in relation to enemies. Psalm 57 pictures a righteous person's hands washed in a sinner's blood after vengeance. The graphic victory images are compared while preserving foot, hand and dog distinctions.

relationship: Women with tambourines accompany victory praise
rationale: The psalm's musicians include young women beating tambourines. Exodus describes Miriam and women with timbrels and dances, leading praise after the sea deliverance. This is a specific musical comparison, not an identification of the psalm's procession with Miriam's occasion.

relationship: Blessing the Lord in assemblies
rationale: Both explicitly locate blessing the Lord in assemblies. Psalm 67 addresses the assembled community from Israel's springs; Psalm 25 states the individual speaker's intention to bless there. No unexpressed interpretation of springs is needed for this link.

relationship: Foreign royalty and gifts directed toward Jerusalem's worship
rationale: The psalm places kings' gifts in relation to God's sanctuary over Jerusalem. Isaiah addresses Jerusalem and joins kings coming by her light with foreign wealth, offerings and the glorified house of prayer. The comparison preserves their distinct descriptions of the visitors.

relationship: God ends the pursuit of war
rationale: Psalm 67 asks God to scatter nations that desire wars. Psalm 45 describes Him ending wars to earth's limits and breaking their weapons. The connection rests on the explicit war clause, without identifying the psalm's reed beasts, bulls or silver-tested people.

relationship: Egypt and Ethiopia brought into acknowledgment of Israel's God
rationale: Psalm 67 names Egyptian envoys and Ethiopia hastening its hand toward God. Isaiah brings Egypt's labor and Ethiopians' trade into a scene of people in bonds acknowledging Israel's God. The named nations and divine acknowledgment correspond, while the differing modes of approach remain distinct.

relationship: Kingdoms sing to the God who rules nations
rationale: The psalm addresses earth's kingdoms with commands to sing and make music. Psalm 46 repeats the command to make music and explains that God is King of all earth and reigns over nations. The international kingship supplies the specific scope of the praise.

relationship: The divine voice speaks with power
rationale: Psalm 67 describes the heavenly rider giving a voice of power. Psalm 28 places the Lord's voice over waters and declares its strength and magnificence. The voice-and-power correspondence does not replace the rider's actual direction toward the east.

relationship: God gives strength to His people
rationale: Both explicitly promise that God or the Lord gives strength to His people. Psalm 67 adds strengthening and blessing God; Psalm 28 adds His blessing of peace upon the people.

relationship: The distinctive heading concerning those who will be changed
rationale: Both headings contain concerning those who will be changed. Psalm 68 names David, while Psalm 44 names the sons of Korah and adds understanding and the beloved. The shared heading is recorded without deciding what change it denotes.

relationship: Dangerous waters reach the speaker's life
rationale: Psalm 68 cries for rescue because waters reach the soul. Jonah describes sea depths, engulfing waves and water up to his life. The shared drowning lament is compared without locating the psalmist inside Jonah's sea creature.

relationship: Mud and the absence or restoration of firm footing
rationale: Psalm 68 describes being stuck in deep mud with no firm ground. Psalm 39 recalls rescue from muddy slime followed by feet set upon a rock. The contrasting danger and rescue concern the same mud-and-footing imagery.

relationship: Failing eyes while waiting for divine help
rationale: Psalm 68 says the eyes failed from hoping in God. Psalm 118 joins a failing soul and eyes with hope in God's word and a question about comfort. Both portray the bodily strain of prolonged expectation.

relationship: Without-cause hatred cited in the Gospel
rationale: John explicitly cites the scriptural words They hated Me without cause as fulfilled in hostility toward Jesus. Psalm 68 contains that without-cause hatred language; the link does not assert that this wording occurs nowhere else or extend the citation to every statement in the psalm.

relationship: Wrongdoing is fully exposed before God
rationale: Psalm 68 acknowledges that God knows the speaker's folly and that offenses are not concealed. Psalm 89 places communal lawless deeds before Him. Both confess divine knowledge of wrongdoing, without replacing the latter's actual age wording with secret sins.

relationship: Those waiting for God and the prospect of shame
rationale: Psalm 68 asks that those waiting for God not be ashamed because of the speaker. Psalm 24 declares that all who wait for Him will not be ashamed. The community and waiting-not-shame formula correspond, while the source adds concern about the speaker's effect on others.

relationship: Reproach endured in relation to God and His words
rationale: Psalm 68 says the speaker endured reproach on God's account. Jeremiah likewise asks God to recognize reproach received concerning Him from those rejecting His words. The connection preserves the distinct speakers and their stated relation to God.

relationship: Kinship becomes estrangement
rationale: Psalm 68 describes estrangement from brothers and being foreign to the mother's sons. Job describes brothers withdrawing, close people failing to acknowledge him and being a foreigner in the household. Both give concrete family and household alienation.

relationship: Zeal for God's house remembered concerning Jesus
rationale: After Jesus acts in the temple, His disciples remember the written statement about zeal for God's house consuming Him. It corresponds to the psalm's zeal devouring the speaker; the difference between remembered future wording and the psalm's past statement is preserved.

relationship: The reproach clause applied explicitly to Christ
rationale: Romans quotes the psalm's reproaches falling upon the speaker and applies it to Christ not pleasing Himself. This is an explicit use of the source's second clause in an argument about bearing others' weaknesses.

relationship: The soul humbled in fasting amid hostility
rationale: Psalm 68 says the speaker bowed the soul down in fasting and received reproach. Psalm 34 describes sackcloth and humbling the soul with fasting when others troubled him. Both connect fasting and the humbled soul with hostile treatment.

relationship: The sufferer becomes other people's repeated tale
rationale: Psalm 68 says the speaker became a proverb to others. Job describes himself as their lyre and their repeated tale. The comparison concerns a person's suffering becoming material for others' speech and ridicule, not a shared sackcloth detail.

relationship: The sufferer made into a mocking song
rationale: Psalm 68 says wine-drinkers sang about the speaker. Lamentations calls its speaker a laughingstock and the people's psalm all day. Both turn personal distress into the community's mocking song, with different groups named.

relationship: Prayer and hearing at a time of favor
rationale: Psalm 68 turns toward God at a time of favor and asks to be heard in salvation. Isaiah speaks of hearing at an acceptable time and help on a day of salvation. The petition and divine assurance share this time-and-salvation formulation.

relationship: Same-chapter petition answers the opening mud-and-water lament
rationale: The later request to be saved from clay and watery depth answers the earlier description of being stuck in mud without firm ground and entering sea depths. The repeated concrete images connect the lament's description to its explicit petition.

relationship: The closing pit and engulfing water threaten life
rationale: Psalm 68 asks that water not drown the speaker and a well not close its mouth over him. Lamentations describes life in a pit under a stone, water over the head and a cry from the lowest pit. The confinement and drowning images supply the parallel without equating historical events.

relationship: Appeal to the abundance of divine compassions
rationale: Both address God through His mercy and abundance of compassions. Psalm 68 asks for hearing and a favorable look; Psalm 50 asks for the blotting out of wrongdoing. The shared appeal is retained with those different requests.

relationship: The afflicted ask for an unturned face and a quick hearing
rationale: Both ask God not to turn His face away and to hear quickly in affliction. The combination of face, distress and urgent hearing is explicit in both passages.

relationship: No comforter is found in grief
rationale: The psalmist looks for someone to grieve and comfort but finds none. Lamentations describes weeping Jerusalem without a comforter among those who love her. The contrast between expected companions and absent consolation is shared, while the latter personifies a city.

relationship: Gall offered to the sufferer
rationale: The psalm names gall given for food; Matthew describes wine mixed with gall offered to Jesus before crucifixion. The gall correspondence is explicit, while Matthew's drink and Jesus' refusal are not substituted for the source's food clause.

relationship: Thirst and sour wine in the Passion
rationale: John links Jesus' stated thirst with Scripture's completion and the sour wine brought to His mouth. This corresponds to the psalm's sour wine given for thirst, without claiming John explicitly names this psalm in the passage.

relationship: The table-as-trap curse quoted as David's words
rationale: Romans attributes to David the table becoming a snare, trap, stumbling block and repayment. The psalm supplies the table, trap, repayment and stumbling-block clause; Romans adds snare in its quoted form.

relationship: Darkened eyes and the continually bent back quoted
rationale: Romans repeats the request for eyes darkened so as not to see and a continually bent back. This directly corresponds to both bodily images in the source unit.

relationship: Divine fury poured on oppressors
rationale: The psalm asks that God's anger be poured upon its adversaries. Jeremiah likewise asks for fury poured upon nations and generations that consumed Jacob. The shared pouring-of-fury request is distinguished from the different descriptions of its recipients.

relationship: The deserted dwelling clause applied to Judas
rationale: Acts quotes a deserted dwelling with no inhabitant in Peter's discussion of Judas. The psalm uses their homestead and dwellings, while Acts uses his dwelling. The singular application is preserved alongside the source's plural wording.

relationship: Adversaries add affliction beyond divine displeasure
rationale: Psalm 68 accuses opponents of persecuting the one God struck and adding pain to His wounded. Zechariah condemns nations that joined in attack to bring evils when God was a little angry. Both distinguish God's displeasure from adversaries' additional assault.

relationship: Erasure from God's book
rationale: The psalm asks that adversaries be erased from the book of the living and not recorded with the righteous. Exodus contains Moses' request to be blotted from God's book and God's response about blotting out sinners. The book-and-erasure language is shared without equating Moses with the psalm's adversaries.

relationship: Praise preferred to animal offerings
rationale: The preceding song of praise is said to please God more than a horned, hoofed calf. Psalm 49 questions eating bulls' flesh and drinking goats' blood and commands a sacrifice of praise. Both distinguish praise from the material animals offered.

relationship: Seeking God is joined to living
rationale: The psalm calls people to seek God so their soul will live. Amos explicitly repeats Seek Me and you will live and Seek the Lord and live. The command and promised life closely correspond.

relationship: God hears the lowly and those in bonds
rationale: Psalm 68 joins hearing the needy with not despising His bound ones. Psalm 101 joins regard for the lowly's prayer with hearing those in bonds. Both connect divine attention to poverty and imprisonment.

relationship: Earth, watery depths and creeping creatures summoned to praise
rationale: Psalm 68 calls the sea and all creeping things in it, along with heaven and earth, to praise. Psalm 148 calls the earth, deeps and creeping things into its creation-wide praise. The sea/deeps and creature groups form the particular comparison.

relationship: Jerusalem and Judea's cities rebuilt and inhabited
rationale: Psalm 68 anticipates Zion's salvation, the building of Judea's cities and renewed dwelling. Isaiah likewise promises inhabited Jerusalem and rebuilt cities of Judea. The named city region and restoration of habitation correspond.

relationship: God's servants and offspring inherit and dwell
rationale: The psalm promises possession to the servants' offspring and dwelling to those loving God's name. Isaiah promises inheritance and dwelling for offspring from Jacob and Judah, the chosen and God's slaves. Both join descent, service, inheritance and residence.

relationship: The heading for remembrance
rationale: Both headings name David and include for remembrance. Psalm 37 additionally specifies the Sabbath; Psalm 69's following source unit continues with saving and help. No particular commemorated event is assumed.

relationship: The shared opening plea of a repeated closing passage
rationale: Psalm 69's plea for God to attend to help corresponds to Psalm 39's request that the Lord attend to helping and rescue. It begins a five-unit sequence in Psalm 69 that closely parallels Psalm 39's closing five units.

relationship: Pursuers shamed and turned backward in corresponding clauses
rationale: Both ask that those seeking the speaker's soul be ashamed and that those wishing evil turn backward in disgrace. This is the next corresponding unit in the two passages' parallel sequence.

relationship: The taunting Well response reversed into shame
rationale: Both connect an immediate reversal into shame with people uttering a doubled Well or Well done taunt. The precise taunt wording differs slightly and is retained as supplied.

relationship: Seekers rejoice and salvation-lovers magnify God
rationale: Both join rejoicing seekers of God with those loving His salvation and their continuing call that God or the Lord be magnified. The sequence and paired groups closely correspond.

relationship: The poor speaker names God helper and asks Him not to delay
rationale: Both close with the speaker poor and needy, God as helper, and the request not to delay. Psalm 69 says rescuer and asks for help; Psalm 39 says defender and declares the Lord's care.

relationship: Hope in God and the plea never to be disgraced
rationale: The running prayer in Psalm 70 closely matches Psalm 30's opening hope in the Lord and request never to be put to shame. This link does not resolve Psalm 70's additional Jonadab-and-captivity heading.

relationship: Righteous rescue and the inclining ear
rationale: Both couple rescue in God's righteousness with His inclining an ear to the speaker. Psalm 70 gathers in one unit wording spread over the two Psalm 30 units.

relationship: God as a defending place of refuge
rationale: Both ask for or declare God as a protecting refuge that saves the speaker. Psalm 30 joins protecting God, house of refuge and stronghold; Psalm 70 joins defending God, fortified place and firm support.

relationship: Rescue from the hand of wrongdoers
rationale: Psalm 70 asks rescue from the hand of a sinner and one acting lawlessly. Jeremiah records God's promise to rescue from the hand of evil people and ransom from pestilent people. The repeated hand-of-wrongdoers formulation connects petition and assurance.

relationship: Divine support beginning in the mother's womb
rationale: Both describe dependence upon God from the womb and mother's belly. Psalm 70 says supported and sheltered; Psalm 21 says drawn out and cast upon God. The birth-stage dependence is explicit without identifying the speakers.

relationship: God's care sought into old age
rationale: The psalm asks not to be cast away or forsaken when age weakens the speaker. Isaiah addresses those carried from the belly and promises divine bearing, rescue and salvation into advanced age. The whole-life care provides a particular answer-pattern to the petition.

relationship: Enemies gather and plan against the speaker's life
rationale: Psalm 70 describes enemies watching the soul and plotting together. Psalm 30 describes people gathering against the speaker and planning to take his soul. The shared collective conspiracy is explicit.

relationship: The enemy taunt denies rescue from God
rationale: Psalm 70's enemies declare God has forsaken the speaker and that there is no rescuer. Psalm 3 reports the claim that there is no salvation for him in his God. Neither hostile assertion is treated as the narrator's judgment.

relationship: God asked not to put His help far away
rationale: Both combine a request against divine distance with a call to attend to help or support. The paired distance-and-attending clauses supply the correspondence.

relationship: Slanderers clothed in shame
rationale: Psalm 70 asks that slanderers and evil-seekers wrap themselves in shame and confusion. Psalm 108 asks that slanderers wear humiliation and wrap shame like a double cloak. The clothing image and the slanderers' role correspond.

relationship: Proclaiming salvation without literary learning
rationale: The psalmist proclaims divine salvation while saying he did not know literary learning. Acts places the proclamation of salvation alongside recognition that Peter and John were unlettered ordinary men. The comparison concerns proclamation and learning, without identifying the psalmist as either apostle.

relationship: Divine mighty acts announced to the coming generation
rationale: Psalm 70 asks for continued support until God's power and righteousness are announced to the coming generation. Psalm 77 describes transmission of His mighty acts to children yet to be born so they will hope in Him. The intergenerational purpose is explicit in both.

relationship: Who is like God who does great wonders
rationale: The psalm's question Who is like Thee accompanies God's great acts. Exodus asks the same incomparable-God question and describes Him working wonders. The question and divine acts occur together in both.

relationship: God makes alive and brings up from below
rationale: The psalm recalls renewed life and being brought up from earth's depths after grievous troubles. Hannah's song declares that the Lord gives life and brings up from Hades. The rescue images correspond without turning the psalm's earth-depths language into an unqualified account of bodily resurrection.

relationship: Deliverance from the lowest depth
rationale: Psalm 70 repeats being brought up from earth's depths, now alongside comfort. Psalm 85 names deliverance of the soul from lowest Hades. The upward rescue corresponds while earth's depths and Hades remain the distinct supplied expressions.

relationship: Instrumental praise of the faithful God
rationale: Psalm 70 joins acknowledging God's truth with instruments and a lyre. Psalm 32 calls for lyre and psaltery praise and grounds it in the upright word and faithful works of the Lord. Both connect instrumental praise with divine truth or faithfulness.

relationship: The redeemed rejoice in praise
rationale: The psalm's redeemed soul and singing lips exult. Isaiah places the redeemed on the holy way and describes returning people with praise, exultation and gladness. Individual and communal portrayals share redemption expressed in joyful praise.

relationship: The tongue praises righteousness after the adversaries' shame
rationale: Psalm 70 joins opponents' shame with the tongue's all-day meditation on God's righteousness. Psalm 34 moves from enemies' shame and humiliation to the same tongue, righteousness and all-day praise wording.

relationship: Solomon asks for the ability to judge God's people
rationale: The psalm's title names Solomon and asks God to give judgment and righteousness to the king and king's son. First Kings recounts David's son Solomon requesting a hearing heart to judge the people in righteousness and God's answer. The link does not settle every later royal image in the psalm.

relationship: Royal judgment attends to the lowly and righteousness
rationale: Psalm 71 asks for righteous judgment of God's people and justice for the poor. Isaiah's shoot from Jesse judges the cause of the lowly and wears righteousness. The comparison concerns the stated character of rule, without identifying the two portraits solely from this unit.

relationship: The vulnerable defended against unjust aggressors
rationale: Psalm 71 describes saving the needy's children and humbling the false accuser. Job recalls fatherly care for the powerless, investigating cases and taking plunder from unjust people's teeth. This is a concrete claimed practice of protective justice, not a claim that Job is the king in the psalm.

relationship: Royal endurance measured by sun and moon
rationale: Psalm 71 describes the king enduring alongside sun and moon through generations. Psalm 88's covenant speech about David describes enduring seed and a throne like sun and moon. The astronomical comparison of royal duration is shared.

relationship: Righteous rule with enduring peace
rationale: Psalm 71 joins the rise of righteousness with abundant peace in the king's days. Isaiah joins the child's rule and limitless peace on David's throne with righteousness and judgment. The supplied Isaiah numbering is 9:5-6.

relationship: The coming king's rule expressed through seas and rivers
rationale: Psalm 71 extends royal rule from sea to sea and river to the inhabited world's ends. Zechariah describes the coming king ruling waters as far as the sea and earth's river outlets. The maritime reach corresponds, but Zechariah is not falsely quoted as containing the psalm's identical sea-to-sea formula.

relationship: Subjection pictured as bowing and licking dust
rationale: Psalm 71 describes Ethiopians falling before the king and enemies licking dust. Isaiah pictures kings and ruling women bowing to Zion and licking the dust of her feet. The bodily image corresponds while the groups and recipient of homage remain distinct.

relationship: Royal gifts from Saba to Solomon
rationale: The psalm anticipates gifts from kings including Saba, under a title naming Solomon. Chronicles recounts Saba's queen bringing and giving gold, spices and stones to Solomon. This illustrates royal gifts from the named region without claiming the single embassy exhausts the psalm's broader language.

relationship: Worldwide homage accompanies enduring royal authority
rationale: Psalm 71 describes all kings bowing and all nations serving the ruler. Daniel's vision gives authority to the one like a son of man and describes all earth's nations worshipping him. The universal homage corresponds without importing a different version of Daniel's vision.

relationship: Rescue of the poor from a powerful person's hand
rationale: Both use the specific rescue of a poor person from a powerful man's hand and help for one lacking a helper. The psalm names the needy; Job names an orphan in its second clause.

relationship: Redemption of vulnerable people amid financial exaction
rationale: The psalm names redemption from interest-taking and injustice. Nehemiah combines purchase of Jewish brothers sold to nations with rebuke of demands against brothers and relinquishment of exaction. This compares economic rescue without asserting that Nehemiah explicitly uses the psalm's interest-taking term.

relationship: Arabia's gold brought to Solomon
rationale: Psalm 71 anticipates Arabia's gold being given to the ruler. Chronicles explicitly records Arabia's kings bringing gold and silver to Solomon. The named region, gift metal and royal recipient supply the connection; the psalm's prayers are not attributed to that narrative.

relationship: Communal flourishing pictured through Lebanon and fruitful growth
rationale: Psalm 71 describes raised fruit beyond Lebanon and people blossoming like grass. Hosea describes Israel blossoming, rooted and fragrant like Lebanon, with spreading branches and fruit. The related human-growth imagery is retained without rewriting Psalm 71's firm support as an absent grain clause.

relationship: Blessing extending to all earth's nations
rationale: The psalm describes all tribes blessed in the ruler and all nations calling him blessed. Genesis promises all earth's nations blessed in Abraham's seed. The shared worldwide blessing formulation is compared without reducing that seed to a single identification from this verse alone.

relationship: God alone works wonders
rationale: Both combine God's uniqueness with His doing wonders. Psalm 71 blesses the God of Israel who alone does wonders; Psalm 85 says He does wondrous things and alone is the great God.

relationship: The whole earth filled with the Lord's glory
rationale: Psalm 71 wishes the whole earth filled with divine glory. Numbers states in the Lord's oath that His glory shall fill all the earth. The same worldwide filling by glory occurs in a doxology and in divine speech.

relationship: A hymn-collection ending alongside a later prayer for David
rationale: The notice says the hymns of David son of Jesse have ended here. A later psalm is nevertheless headed A prayer for David. This compares the collection notice with the later heading without claiming that for David asserts Davidic authorship or that every David-related text ends at Psalm 71.
